hook.line: Tomás has to explain a decision to the staff. Saying what happened is easy; saying what follows from it is where you start to sound like an adult.
hook.es: Las ventas bajaron; por lo tanto, cerramos los lunes.
hook.en: Sales fell; therefore, we close on Mondays.

examples.es: Las ventas bajaron; por lo tanto, cerramos los lunes.
examples.en: Sales fell; therefore, we close on Mondays.

examples.es: Llovió mucho, de modo que nos quedamos en casa.
examples.en: It rained a lot, so we stayed at home.

examples.es: Estaba tan cansado que se durmió.
examples.en: He was so tired that he fell asleep.

examples.es: Hubo tanto ruido que no pude dormir.
examples.en: There was so much noise that I couldn't sleep.

examples.es: Había tanta gente que no había mesas.
examples.en: There were so many people that there were no tables.

examples.es: Hernando habla tan rápido que nadie lo entiende.
examples.en: Hernando talks so fast that nobody understands him.

rule:
Three ways to say what follows from something.

*Por lo tanto* means "therefore". It is the formal one: it comes after a semicolon or a full stop, with a comma after it.

*De modo que* means "so". It is lighter, after a comma: *Llovió, de modo que nos quedamos.* In chat you will hear *así que* even more.

For "so much that", Spanish builds a pair: *tan* + adjective or adverb + *que*, or *tanto* + noun + *que*. *Tanto* matches its noun: *tanto ruido*, *tanta gente*.

English often drops "that": "so tired he slept". Spanish never drops *que*.
smallPrint: Teachers call these consecutive connectors, because they introduce the consequence.

readAndPick.es: Las ventas bajaron; por lo tanto, cerramos los lunes.
options: We close on Mondays, so sales fell.
Sales fell, so we close on Mondays.
Sales fell because we close on Mondays.

readAndPick.es: Llovió mucho, de modo que nos quedamos en casa.
options: It rained a lot, so we stayed at home.
We stayed at home, so it rained a lot.
It rained a lot, but we stayed at home.

readAndPick.es: Estaba tan cansado que se durmió.
options: He was tired, but he didn't sleep.
He fell asleep, so he was tired.
He was so tired that he fell asleep.

readAndPick.es: Hubo tanto ruido que no pude dormir.
options: There was so little noise that I couldn't sleep.
There was so much noise that I couldn't sleep.

readAndPick.es: Es tan caro que no lo compro.
options: It's so expensive that I don't buy it.
It's cheap, so I buy it.
It's so expensive that I bought it.

readAndPick.es: No tengo tiempo; por lo tanto, no voy.
options: I'm not going, so I have no time.
I have time, so I'm going.
I have no time, so I'm not going.

readAndPick.es: Tengo tanto trabajo que no puedo salir.
options: I have so much work that I can't go out.
I have a lot of work, but I can go out.
I can't go out, so I have work.

readAndPick.es: Ella está tan ocupada que no contesta el celular.
options: She's busy, so she answers the phone.
She isn't busy, so she doesn't answer.
She's so busy that she doesn't answer the phone.

readAndPick.es: Hay mucha gente, de modo que no hay mesa.
options: There's no table, so there are lots of people.
There are lots of people, so there's no table.

yourTurn.prompt: There are lots of people, so there's no table. Pick the right link: de modo que or tan.
yourTurn.answer: Hay mucha gente, de modo que no hay mesa.
yourTurn.why: *De modo que* is a "so" that follows a comma; *tan* needs a describing word after it.

yourTurn.prompt: I'm so tired (a woman speaking) that I don't want to cook. Pick the right word: tan or tanto.
yourTurn.answer: Estoy tan cansada que no quiero cocinar.
yourTurn.why: *Cansada* describes you, so the word before it is *tan*.

yourTurn.prompt: There were so many people that there were no tables. Pick the right word: tanta or tan.
yourTurn.answer: Había tanta gente que no había mesas.
yourTurn.why: *Gente* is a noun, so you need *tanta*, and it matches *gente*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type it in Spanish: It's so late that there are no buses anymore.
yourTurn.answer: Es tan tarde que ya no hay buses.
yourTurn.why: *Tarde* works like an adjective here, so *tan* comes before it and *que* after.

yourTurn.prompt: Type it in Spanish: There was so much noise that I couldn't sleep.
yourTurn.answer: Hubo tanto ruido que no pude dormir.
accept: Había tanto ruido que no pude dormir.
yourTurn.why: *Ruido* is masculine, so *tanto*, and *que* introduces the result.

yourTurn.prompt: Join with por lo tanto (formal): No tengo tiempo. No voy.
yourTurn.answer: No tengo tiempo; por lo tanto, no voy.
accept: No tengo tiempo. Por lo tanto, no voy.
No tengo tiempo, por lo tanto, no voy.
yourTurn.why: *Por lo tanto* sits between the two ideas, with a comma after it.

yourTurn.prompt: Join with de modo que: No llegó el pan. No abrimos.
yourTurn.answer: No llegó el pan, de modo que no abrimos.
yourTurn.why: *De modo que* follows a comma and keeps its *que*.

pitfalls.right: Estaba tan cansado que se durmió.
pitfalls.why: English can drop "that", but Spanish keeps *que* every time.

pitfalls.wrong: Había tan gente que no había mesas.
pitfalls.right: Había tanta gente que no había mesas.
pitfalls.why: Before a noun use *tanto* and match it; *tan* is only for adjectives and adverbs.

pitfalls.wrong: Es tanto caro que no lo compro.
pitfalls.right: Es tan caro que no lo compro.
pitfalls.why: *Caro* describes, so it takes the short form *tan*.

pitfalls.wrong: Llovió mucho, de modo nos quedamos en casa.
pitfalls.right: Llovió mucho, de modo que nos quedamos en casa.
pitfalls.why: *De modo que* is one block, and the *que* cannot go missing.

personal: Say something true about your day with *tan… que*, like *estoy tan cansado que…*, or with *de modo que*.
